chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:

Regarding a man who went to another man and said: 'So-and-so sent me to you to send such and such [amount/goods] to him.' The man gave it to him and believed him. Later, the sender met the recipient and said to him: 'Your messenger came to me, so I sent with him such and such.' The recipient said: 'I did not send him, and he did not bring me anything.' The messenger claimed that he had been sent and had delivered it to him. The recipient said: 'If evidence is found against him that he was not sent, his hand will be cut off. If no evidence is found, he will take an oath by Allah that he did not send him, and the other party will recover the money from the messenger.' I asked: 'What if he claims that need compelled him to do so?' He said: 'His hand will be cut off, because he stole a man's property.' The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as referring to one who is known for this, by scheming against the wealth of Muslims; it is permissible for the Imam to cut off his hand, because he is a corrupter in the land, not because he is a thief, because this is a stratagem (hi'lah) and not a theft that requires cutting off [the hand].
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between cutting off the hand for theft versus for scheming against wealth in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies the distinction between standard theft (sariqah) and fraud (ghash/tahwil) by a messenger, noting that hand amputation applies to the latter only if the individual is known for habitual scheming against Muslims' wealth. It highlights the Imam's discretionary authority to treat such habitual fraudsters as 'mufsidun' (corrupters) in the land, thereby extending the penalty beyond the strict conditions of ordinary theft. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that context and reputation can elevate a civil wrong to a capital offense.
